entries.topic: Electoral College architecture: Article II, 12th Amendment, winner-take-all, Maine and Nebraska

claims.text: CRS (5 May 2026): 538 electoral votes, 270 to win; each state gets electors equal to its House plus Senate seats; the 23rd Amendment gives DC three; 3 to 54 (California) for 2024 and 2028; 48 states use winner-take-all ('general ticket'); Maine and Nebraska give one vote per congressional district and two to the statewide winner; contingent election: House picks the President with one vote per state delegation, Senate picks the VP; 1824 House chose John Quincy Adams

CRS: arguments for change call the system 'antiquated and undemocratic'; defenders say the Framers chose it to emphasise the states' role in federalism; recent amendment proposals (H.J.Res. 102, 119th; H.J.Res. 227 and S.J.Res. 121, 118th) 'have not substantially advanced beyond introduction'

12th Amendment: electors name President and Vice President in 'distinct ballots'; a winner needs 'a majority of the whole number of Electors appointed'; otherwise the House chooses from the top three, 'the representation from each state having one vote'; Senate chooses VP from top two; adopted after the 1800 Jefferson-Burr tie

FairVote: Virginia switched to a statewide popular vote in 1800; Jefferson: 'it is folly & worse than folly for the other 6 not to do it'; Massachusetts switched to legislative choice to secure votes for Adams; by 1836 all states except South Carolina used statewide winner-take-all; SC's legislature chose electors until after the Civil War; by 1872 all states held a popular vote; Colorado's legislature chose in 1876; driven by partisan advantage

Maine adopted the district method for 1972, Nebraska for 1992; NE-2 went to Obama in 2008 (first Democratic electoral vote from Nebraska since 1964); ME-2 to Trump in 2016; in 2020 both districts went to the statewide loser
2024: NE-2 to Harris, ME-2 to Trump (third straight win); a Nebraska Republican effort to return to winner-take-all failed after a key GOP legislator opposed it

entries.topic: Federalist 68's screening role, faithless electors, the Hamilton Electors and Chiafalo v. Washington

claims.text: Federalist 68: the election should be made by 'men most capable of analizing the qualities adapted to the station'; 'every practicable obstacle should be opposed to cabal, intrigue and corruption'; warns of 'the desire in foreign powers to gain an improper ascendant in our councils'; 'Talents for low intrigue and the little arts of popularity may alone suffice' for a single state but not the nation; aim of 'as little opportunity as possible to tumult and disorder'

Chiafalo v. Washington, 6 July 2020: unanimous holding (Kagan for eight; Thomas, joined in part by Gorsuch, concurring in the judgment); states may fine or replace electors who break their pledge; Baca reversed per curiam; 32 states and DC required pledges in 2020, 15 imposed sanctions; electors have pledged to parties since 1796; about one-half of one percent of electoral votes in history went against the home-state winner, none changing an outcome; 'electors are not free agents; they are to vote for the candidate whom the State's voters have chosen'; the 12th Amendment 'made party-line voting safe'
Chiafalo and two other Washington Democratic electors voted for Colin Powell in 2016; each faced a $1,000 fine

Seven faithless electoral votes in 2016: five pledged to Clinton (Mulinix HI for Sanders; Chiafalo, Guerra, John WA for Powell; Satiacum WA for Faith Spotted Eagle), two pledged to Trump (Suprun TX for Kasich; Greene TX for Ron Paul); final 304-227

30 Nov 2016: Democratic electors calling themselves 'Hamilton Electors', citing Federalist 68, asked 37 Republican electors to vote for an alternative Republican so that Trump would fall short of 270 and the House would choose; they acknowledged the plan was unlikely to succeed

entries.topic: Popular-vote splits, 2024 result, campaign concentration, ECRA, NPV compact, the 1969-70 amendment, public opinion

claims.text: 2024: Trump 312 electoral votes, Harris 226; Trump 77,303,568 (49.8%), Harris 75,019,230 (48.3%)
2020: 204 of 212 general-election events (96%) by the major-party tickets were in 12 states; 33 states and DC had none; period 28 Aug-3 Nov 2020; FairVote data
2024: 261 events from the conventions to Election Day; 94% in seven states (AZ, GA, MI, NV, NC, PA, WI); 16 events elsewhere; '32 states didn't receive a single visit'

ECRA 2022: objections need one-fifth of each chamber (1887 Act: one member of each); the VP's role is ministerial; the governor submits the certificate of ascertainment unless state law names another official; expedited judicial review; introduced by Collins on 20 Jul 2022 with Manchin; attached to the omnibus; Senate 68-29 on 22 Dec, House 225-201 on 23 Dec; signed by Biden 23 Dec 2022

NPVIC: Gov. Spanberger signed Virginia's bill on 13 Apr 2026; compact now 18 states plus DC with 222 electoral votes, 48 short of 270; critic Patrick Valencia (now Iowa deputy solicitor general) calls it an effort to 'usurp the constitutionally required electoral procedures'; other scholars argue such a change needs an amendment; supporters cite Article II and expect a court challenge at 270; Virginia's measure advanced after Democrats won full control

Bayh-Celler: House passed direct popular election (40% threshold, runoff otherwise) 339-70 on 18 Sep 1969; Nixon endorsed it on 30 Sep 1969; Senate cloture failed 54-36 on 17 Sep 1970 and 53-34 on 29 Sep 1970, short of two-thirds; opponents mainly southern senators and small-state conservatives of both parties; died with the 91st Congress
Pew (26 Aug-2 Sep 2024, n=9,720): 63% favour a popular-vote system, 35% keep the EC; Democrats about 80%, Republicans 46% (53% keep); Republican support was 27% in November 2016
Gallup (Aug-Sep 2020): 61% favour an amendment for a national popular vote; Democrats 89%, independents 68%, Republicans 23%; support fell below a majority only once, in November 2016 (49% vs 47%)
Gallup (3-15 Sep 2024, n=1,007): 58% favour a popular-vote amendment, 38% keep the EC; Democrats 82%, independents 60%, Republicans 32% (66% keep)

claims.text: Pew (25 Sep 2024): in 2020 Biden won the popular vote by more than 7 million votes, but his Electoral College victory was decided by fewer than 50,000 votes in a few close states

CRS R48936 (5 May 2026): 'On four occasions, the electoral college has produced a presidential winner inconsistent with the national popular vote': 1876, 1888, 2000 and 2016; electors meet on the first Tuesday after the second Wednesday in December (17 December 2024; 19 December 2028)

KNKX 30 Nov 2016: 'Four Democratic electors from Washington and Colorado are leading the effort'; Levi Guerra, 19, of Warden, Wash.: 'it is not an easy thing for me to pledge my vote to a qualified Republican alternative'; target 37 Republican electors before the 19 December vote
